beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Adwait Changan, and this video is about why agents do not actually forget. Today we are going to learn where an agent's memory really lives — and it is not where most people think. Last week we counted what a single tool costs to describe. Now we add them up across a whole run, and find that an agent has no memory at all. It has a budget, and it re-pays that budget every single turn.

props.command: Where does an agent's memory actually live, and what does it cost me per turn?
output: Nowhere. There is no memory — there is a context window.
Every turn re-sends the whole thing from scratch: instructions, tools, history.
So forgetting is not amnesia. It is overflow, and you choose what gets dropped.

beats.narration_text: Here is the whole model, before any example. Every turn, three things compete for one budget. Your instructions and tool definitions — fixed, but re-sent every single time. The history — everything said and observed so far, which only grows. And whatever is left over. That last one is where the answer has to fit.

beats.narration_text: And here is the part people miss. Nothing persists on the model's side. Every turn, the entire thing — instructions, tool definitions, the full history — is packed up and sent again from scratch. The model is not remembering your last turn. You are re-telling it, at full price, every time.

beats.narration_text: So let us actually count it. Two tools from last week plus one system prompt: nine hundred and three characters of instructions, before the agent has done anything at all. Then every observation adds eighty-eight more. Watch the right-hand column. Room to answer is not a constant. It is being spent, turn by turn.

beats.narration_text: Which reframes the whole complaint. When an agent loses the thread halfway through a long task, it did not forget anything. It ran out of room, and something had to be dropped. That is not amnesia. That is overflow.

props.title: Overflow, Not Amnesia
props.body: It did not forget. It ran out of room, and something had to be dropped to make the request fit.

beats.narration_text: Ten lines, and the comment on line four is the one that costs people money. Instructions are fixed — and paid again, every turn. History only grows. Room is just subtraction. Notice there is no memory anywhere in this function, because there is no memory anywhere in the system.

beats.narration_text: So when it does not fit, something gets dropped — and you are the one who chooses what. Drop the oldest turns. Summarise them, and lose the evidence. Leave them out and fetch on demand. Or refuse, and fail loudly. There is no fifth option where everything simply fits forever.

'Refuse and fail loudly' completes the grid; caption closes the door on a fifth option

items: Drop the oldest — cheap, and it forgets the setup
Summarise — keeps the gist, loses the evidence
Retrieve on demand — fetch only what this turn needs
Refuse and fail loudly — the honest option
props.caption: There is no fifth option where everything fits forever.

beats.narration_text: Now the obvious objection: just get a bigger window. So we tested it. Double the budget, and the overflow moves from turn thirteen to turn thirty-six. Double it again, turn eighty-one. It never goes away. History grows linearly and the budget is a constant, so every budget overflows eventually. A bigger window buys you turns. It does not buy a fix.

beats.narration_text: Which gives you three questions to ask of any agent turn, on any project. What is fixed here, and am I re-paying for it every turn. What is growing, and how fast. And when it does not fit, what gets dropped — did I choose that, or did a library choose it for me?

beats.narration_text: And that third question separates the people who ship agents from the people who debug them at midnight. Eviction is a design decision. If you did not make it, it was still made — just not by you.

props.title: Someone Chose. Was It You?
props.body: Eviction is a design decision. If you did not make it, it was still made — by a default, in a library you never read.

beats.narration_text: So, the verdict. An agent has no memory. It has a context window, and every turn re-sends the whole thing from scratch — instructions, tool definitions, and all of the history. What looks like forgetting is overflow: the history grows, the budget does not, and something has to give. A bigger window does not fix that. In our own measurement it moved the overflow from turn thirteen to turn eighty-one, and no further. So eviction is the real design decision. Choose what gets dropped, deliberately — or a default will choose it for you.

props.artifactHeading: There is no memory. There is a budget.
artifactLines: An agent has no memory — it has a context window, re-sent in full every single turn.
Three things compete for it: fixed instructions, growing history, and room to answer.
What looks like forgetting is overflow — history grows, the budget does not.
A bigger window moved our overflow from turn 13 to turn 81. It never removed it.
Eviction is the design decision. Choose what gets dropped, or a default chooses for you.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Take the agent I am building. Count the characters in my system prompt and in every tool definition, then estimate how much each turn adds to the history. Tell me which turn I run out of room on, and what my current code drops when that happens. Run that against your own agent. Most people have never measured the fixed cost — and are surprised how much of the budget is gone before the first turn even starts.

props.command: Take the agent I am building. Count the characters in my system prompt and in every tool definition, then estimate how much each turn adds to the history. Tell me which turn I run out of room on, and what my current code drops when that happens.
output: Most people have never measured the fixed cost — it is larger than they guess.
If it cannot say what gets dropped, you have an eviction policy you did not choose.
